977000.long_answer: Mutations in the X-linked MECP2 gene (located at Xq28) cause Rett syndrome, a neurodevelopmental disorder that shares key clinical features with Pitt-Hopkins syndrome—such as severe intellectual disability, absent or limited speech, distinctive breathing abnormalities (hyperventilation/apnoea episodes), and characteristic facial/hand stereotypies. Because MECP2 resides on the X chromosome and its mutation produces a syndrome mimicking Pitt-Hopkins, it is the gene referred to in the question.

117634.long_answer: Hereditary orotic aciduria results from loss-of-function mutations in the UMPS gene, which encodes the bifunctional enzyme uridine-5′-monophosphate synthase (orotate phosphoribosyl-transferase and OMP decarboxylase). The human UMPS gene is mapped to the long arm of chromosome 3 (3q), so the disease-causing gene resides on chromosome 3.

798201.long_answer: Excess (over-dose) of glucocorticoids produces Cushing’s syndrome. Glucocorticoids have potent anti-inflammatory actions because they stabilize lysosomal membranes and thereby inactivate the hydrolytic enzymes contained within lysosomes. When these steroids are taken in excess, the resulting glucocorticoid surplus manifests clinically as Cushing’s syndrome.

964098.long_answer: Smith–Fineman–Myers syndrome is an X-linked intellectual-developmental disorder caused by pathogenic variants in the HCFC1 gene (Host Cell Factor C1). Mutations in HCFC1 disrupt its role as a transcriptional co-regulator during neurodevelopment, leading to the characteristic features of the syndrome, including skeletal manifestations such as scoliosis.

167202.long_answer: Mutations in the PANK2 gene abolish or greatly reduce the activity of the mitochondrial enzyme pantothenate kinase 2, the first, rate-limiting enzyme in coenzyme A biosynthesis. Loss of this enzyme causes pantothenate kinase-associated neurodegeneration (PKAN), a form of NBIA that commonly manifests with dystonia and spasticity.

256633.long_answer: Phenylketonuria (PKU) most commonly results from mutations in the phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH) gene. The PAH gene is mapped to chromosome 12 (12q23.2), not chromosome 17. Therefore, the statement that the gene causing phenylketonuria is located on chromosome 17 is incorrect.

588585.long_answer: Mutations in the EDA gene, which encodes the signalling protein ectodysplasin-A, cause X-linked hypohidrotic (anhidrotic) ectodermal dysplasia. Because ectodermal dysplasia impairs the development of exocrine glands derived from surface ectoderm, patients have markedly reduced salivary, lacrimal and other mucous secretions. This results in dryness and dysfunction of multiple mucous membranes, notably those of the mouth and eyes, illustrating why an EDA mutation leads to disease affecting these tissues.

463880.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the X-linked TIMM8A (also called DDP1) gene cause Mohr-Tranebjaerg syndrome—an inherited disorder whose name begins with “M” and is clinically marked by early-onset sensorineural hearing loss followed by progressive dystonia and other neurodegenerative features. TIMM8A encodes a mitochondrial inner-membrane protein; its deficiency impairs mitochondrial protein import, leading to the auditory and movement abnormalities characteristic of the disease.

813361.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the COL2A1 gene, which encodes type II collagen, cause spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia congenita—a skeletal dysplasia marked by short stature and characteristic vertebral anomalies (e.g., platyspondyly, odontoid hypoplasia). Thus, a COL2A1 mutation is the genetic change linked to a condition producing both skeletal dysplasia and vertebral abnormalities.

498280.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the DHCR7 gene cause Smith-Lemli-Opitz syndrome. DHCR7 encodes 7-dehydrocholesterol reductase, the enzyme that converts 7-dehydrocholesterol to cholesterol. Loss of this activity leads to markedly elevated 7-dehydrocholesterol (and 8-dehydrocholesterol) with reduced cholesterol levels in plasma. Measuring these plasma sterol concentrations (or their ratios) is the standard biochemical test used to diagnose the disorder, directly linking DHCR7 to a condition identifiable by plasma sterol evaluation.

163063.long_answer: Genes encoding classical-pathway complement components such as C1q, C2 and C4 are annotated by the Gene Ontology project under the classical pathway of the complement system. Homozygous deficiency of any of these genes markedly increases the risk of developing the autoimmune disease systemic lupus erythematosus, making SLE the canonical autoimmune disorder linked to classical‐pathway complement gene deficiency.

886864.long_answer: Bordetella pertussis is a Gram-negative bacterium that causes pertussis (whooping cough). The infection begins with a catarrhal phase marked by mild, common-cold-like symptoms (runny nose, mild fever, cough). After 1–2 weeks it progresses to the paroxysmal phase, characterized by repetitive, forceful coughing fits followed by the classic inspiratory 'whoop.' These clinical stages and symptoms are distinctive for disease caused by B. pertussis.

168507.long_answer: Mutations in the SCN1A gene, which encodes the α-subunit of the voltage-gated sodium channel Nav1.1, cause Dravet syndrome (severe myoclonic epilepsy of infancy). This epileptic encephalopathy is characterized by febrile and afebrile seizures beginning in the first year of life, along with developmental delay and other neurological deficits, making SCN1A mutation a well-established genetic cause of a syndrome in which seizures are a core feature.

685394.long_answer: The palmoplantar keratoderma known as Mal de Meleda is caused by pathogenic mutations in the SLURP1 gene. The condition was first described in inhabitants of the Croatian island of Mljet (historically called Meleda), and the disease name reflects this geographic origin.

741439.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the CHD7 gene cause CHARGE syndrome, a multisystem developmental disorder in which ocular abnormalities are frequent. Strabismus (misalignment of the eyes) is reported in a significant proportion of individuals with CHARGE syndrome, linking CHD7 mutations directly to a condition that includes strabismus as a clinical feature.

256524.long_answer: Mycobacterium tuberculosis, the causative agent of tuberculosis, can infect the spine, producing ‘Pott’s disease’ (tuberculous spondylitis). This form of TB leads to granulomatous inflammation and destruction of the vertebrae, resulting in vertebral pain, deformity, and potential neurological complications.

554461.long_answer: Buschke–Ollendorff syndrome is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the LEMD3 (MAN1) gene. LEMD3 encodes an inner nuclear membrane protein containing a LEM domain, so pathogenic variants directly disturb nuclear-envelope structure and related TGF-β/BMP signalling pathways.

731205.long_answer: Woodhouse–Sakati syndrome results from biallelic mutations in the DCAF17 gene (formerly C2orf37). This gene is situated on the long arm of human chromosome 2 at cytogenetic band 2q31.1, making chromosome 2 the locus responsible for the disorder.

453929.long_answer: Rothmund–Thomson syndrome is caused by pathogenic variants in the RECQL4 helicase gene. The RECQL4 gene is located on chromosome 8q24. Therefore, the gene responsible for Rothmund–Thomson syndrome resides on chromosome 8.

196541.long_answer: The glycogen storage disease initially labeled as type XI (Fanconi-Bickel syndrome) was later removed from the classical glycogen-storage-disease group because it results from a defect in the glucose transporter protein GLUT2 rather than an enzyme of glycogen metabolism. This disorder is caused by pathogenic variants in the SLC2A2 gene, which encodes the GLUT2 transport protein.

362139.long_answer: Cantú syndrome is chiefly produced by gain-of-function mutations in the ABCC9 gene, which encodes the SUR2 subunit of ATP-sensitive potassium channels. ABCC9 is situated on chromosome 12p12.1. The best-characterised locus for familial patent ductus arteriosus (PDA1) likewise maps to chromosome 12, placing ABCC9 on the same chromosome as the gene implicated in patent ductus arteriosus.

174158.long_answer: Mutations in the RYR1 gene, which encodes the skeletal-muscle ryanodine receptor Ca2+-release channel, are the well-established genetic cause of malignant hyperthermia—a pharmacogenetic anesthetic reaction extensively covered in eMedicine/Medscape. Defective RYR1 channels allow excessive sarcoplasmic Ca2+ release when patients are exposed to triggering agents (e.g., volatile anesthetics, succinylcholine), precipitating the hypermetabolic crisis that defines the condition.

568329.long_answer: Adenine phosphoribosyltransferase (APRT) deficiency is caused by pathogenic variants in the APRT gene. Molecular mapping and sequence analysis have located the human APRT gene to the long arm of chromosome 16 (16q24.3). Therefore, the genetic defect responsible for APRT deficiency resides on chromosome 16.

421855.long_answer: Mutations in the FGFR2 gene cause Apert syndrome, a craniosynostosis disorder whose characteristic clinical triad includes craniosynostosis, mid-face hypoplasia, and complex syndactyly of the hands and feet. FGFR2 (fibroblast growth factor receptor 2) gain-of-function mutations disrupt signaling pathways that regulate bone growth and suture fusion, leading to premature fusion of cranial sutures and the syndactyly phenotype.

765650.long_answer: The myeloperoxidase (MPO) gene resides on chromosome 17 (17q23). Mutations in MPO cause inherited myeloperoxidase deficiency, and neutrophils lacking functional MPO are unable to generate reactive oxygen species–dependent neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) when challenged with Candida albicans, linking the defect in NET formation to chromosome 17.

432468.long_answer: Mutations in the HPSE2 gene, located on chromosome 10q23-q24, cause urofacial (Ochoa) syndrome. This syndrome classically presents with a paradoxical or inverted smile due to abnormal facial nerve control and with severe urinary tract dysfunction (neurogenic bladder, incontinence, or retention), linking HPSE2 mutations directly to the described clinical picture.

921739.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the SEPN1 gene, which encodes the endoplasmic-reticulum protein selenoprotein N, cause ‘SEPN1-related myopathy’ (also called rigid-spine muscular dystrophy 1). This congenital muscular dystrophy presents in infancy with axial muscle weakness leading to marked spinal rigidity and progressive scoliosis, together with later respiratory insufficiency, firmly linking SEPN1 mutations to the described clinical phenotype.

405791.long_answer: The earliest published description of what is now called pilonidal disease was made by the English surgeon Herbert Mayo in 1833, when he reported sacrococcygeal sinuses that contained hair. Although Robert Hodges later coined the term “pilonidal” in 1880, Mayo’s 1833 report is recognized as the first account of the condition.

281543.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the ABCC8 gene, which encodes the SUR1 subunit of the pancreatic β-cell KATP channel, cause congenital hyperinsulinism. This condition is characterized by inappropriate insulin secretion that drives blood glucose below normal levels, resulting in recurrent hypoglycemia.

603161.long_answer: The rare laryngo-onycho-cutaneous (Shabbir) syndrome observed almost exclusively in Punjabi Muslim families is caused by homozygous loss-of-function mutations in the LAMA3 gene, which encodes the α3 chain of laminin-332. Defective laminin-332 impairs epithelial basement-membrane integrity, leading to the characteristic abnormalities of the laryngeal mucosa, nails, and skin seen in this disorder.

722977.long_answer: I-cell disease (mucolipidosis II) results from a severe deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme N-acetylglucosamine-1-phosphotransferase. The enzyme’s catalytic α and β subunits are both encoded by the GNPTAB gene. Mutations in GNPTAB abolish production of these subunits, eliminating phosphotransferase activity and leading to the characteristic cellular inclusions of I-cell disease.

819338.long_answer: Cantú syndrome is caused by gain-of-function mutations in the ABCC9 gene (encoding the SUR2 subunit of ATP-sensitive potassium channels). The ABCC9 gene is mapped to the short arm of human chromosome 12 (12p12.1), so the causal gene for Cantú syndrome is located on chromosome 12.

909361.long_answer: Phenylketonuria is caused by pathogenic variants in the PAH gene (phenylalanine hydroxylase), which is located on the long arm of human chromosome 12 at cytogenetic band 12q23.2. Therefore, the causative gene for phenylketonuria resides on chromosome 12.

486589.long_answer: The disorder is Hunter syndrome (mucopolysaccharidosis type II), an X-linked recessive lysosomal-storage disease that presents with progressive intellectual disability and a pigmentary retinopathy resembling retinitis pigmentosa. It was first described in 1917 by the Scottish physician-geneticist Charles Hunter, after whom the condition is named.

950736.long_answer: Mutations in the XK gene cause McLeod syndrome. Loss of the Kx membrane protein alters red-cell membrane stability, producing acanthocytes (spur cells) and leading to chronic hemolytic anemia.

376087.long_answer: Cartilage–hair hypoplasia (an autosomal-recessive form of dwarfism) is caused by pathogenic variants in the non-coding RNA gene RMRP, which is mapped to the short arm of chromosome 9 (9p). Thus, chromosome 9 is the chromosome associated with the gene responsible for cartilage–hair hypoplasia.

403405.long_answer: The childhood epileptic aphasia known as Landau-Kleffner syndrome was first reported in 1957 by neurologist William M. Landau and speech pathologist Frank R. Kleffner. Because Landau was the neurologist in the pair, the eponym honours him for the condition marked by sudden or progressive loss of language (aphasia) and characteristic epileptiform abnormalities on electroencephalography in children.

570370.long_answer: The earliest clinical description of the rapidly progressive dementia now known as Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease—a prototypical human prion disease—was published in 1920 by the German neurologist Hans Gerhard Creutzfeldt. His report preceded the similar case series of Alfons Maria Jakob and established the syndrome that links prion infection to severe, fatal dementia.

625967.long_answer: In Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome—the genetic condition marked by microcornea, early-onset glaucoma, and hypoplastic or absent frontal sinuses—systemic health is typically unaffected, so life expectancy is normal. The chief risk is ocular: uncontrolled congenital glaucoma can lead to progressive visual loss. With appropriate ophthalmic surveillance and treatment, vision can often be preserved, making the overall prognosis favorable apart from potential eye complications.

406439.long_answer: No contextual information was provided to identify the specific gene. Please supply the relevant background so that the correct gene associated with brachial amelia and cleft lip can be determined.

401153.long_answer: Pathogenic, loss-of-function mutations in the GREB1L gene have been repeatedly documented in families where the fetus presents with bilateral renal agenesis—a condition in which neither kidney forms (Potter sequence). GREB1L encodes a transcriptional co-activator required for the initiation of ureteric bud outgrowth; when GREB1L is disrupted, this critical first step of metanephric kidney development fails, leading to complete absence of both kidneys.

645798.long_answer: Mutations in the TPO gene (thyroid peroxidase) impair thyroid-hormone synthesis, producing thyroid peroxidase deficiency. This condition is classified as Congenital Iodine Deficiency Syndrome type 2 and manifests clinically as congenital hypothyroidism with goiter. The resulting lack of thyroid hormone during growth leads to pronounced growth failure and clinically significant short stature, establishing TPO as the gene linking both short stature and congenital iodine deficiency syndrome.

869040.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the RASA1 gene cause capillary malformation–arteriovenous malformation (CM-AVM) syndrome. This disorder produces diffuse, reticulated capillary malformations and telangiectasias that closely mimic the marbled vascular pattern of cutis marmorata telangiectatica congenita (CMTC), leading to diagnostic confusion between the two conditions.

285846.long_answer: The gene responsible for pseudoachondroplasia was first pinpointed in 1995 by a research team at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA). Their work showed that mutations in the COMP (cartilage oligomeric matrix protein) gene on chromosome 19 cause the disorder, providing the molecular explanation for this form of dwarfism.

360345.long_answer: Tricuspid (and mitral) valve prolapse can occur in Marfan syndrome, an autosomal-dominant connective-tissue disorder caused by pathogenic variants in the FBN1 gene located on chromosome 15q21.1. Hence, chromosome 15 is the chromosome classically associated with this genetic condition that includes tricuspid valve prolapse among its cardiovascular manifestations.

942664.long_answer: Mutations or rearrangements in the OPN1LW gene, which encodes the long-wavelength (red) cone opsin and is located on Xq28 of the X chromosome, cause X-linked red-green color vision deficiency (a form of color blindness).

660560.long_answer: Acute intermittent porphyria is caused by deficiency of the heme-biosynthetic enzyme porphobilinogen deaminase (also called hydroxymethylbilane synthase). This enzymatic defect leads to accumulation of neurotoxic precursors such as aminolevulinic acid and porphobilinogen, which can provoke neurological manifestations including abdominal pain, neuropathy, psychiatric changes, and seizures.

579800.long_answer: Heterozygous mutations in the COL2A1 gene, particularly those that alter the alternatively spliced exon 2 expressed in the eye but not in cartilage, cause the ocular-only form of Stickler syndrome. This condition presents with progressive reduction in visual acuity and a very high lifetime risk of rhegmatogenous retinal detachments, while the extra-ocular systemic manifestations (craniofacial, auditory, skeletal) typical of classic Stickler syndrome are absent.

674083.long_answer: Mutations in the DLL3 gene disrupt the Notch signaling pathway that controls somite segmentation during embryonic development. This leads to the vertebral and rib malformations characteristic of spondylocostal dysostosis, commonly called Jarcho-Levin syndrome, whose clinical picture routinely includes congenital scoliosis.

271305.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the RPE65 gene cause Leber congenital amaurosis type 2 and some forms of early-onset retinitis pigmentosa. Loss of RPE65 disrupts the visual (retinoid) cycle in retinal pigment epithelial cells, leading to rapid photoreceptor degeneration and progressive visual impairment that can culminate in childhood or adolescent blindness.

656918.long_answer: Heterozygous loss-of-function mutations or microdeletions of the NSD1 gene (located at 5q35) are responsible for Sotos (cerebral gigantism) syndrome, whose core clinical features include prenatal/neonatal overgrowth with macrosomia, prominent macrocephaly, and characteristic dysmorphic facial features.

741449.long_answer: Patients with lysinuric protein intolerance frequently show markedly elevated serum ferritin concentrations. Ferritin is the intracellular iron-storage protein, and its rise (hyperferritinemia) reflects the chronic inflammatory/immune activation that accompanies this metabolic disorder.

470392.long_answer: The severe color-blindness disorder with markedly reduced visual acuity (blue-cone monochromacy) is caused by mutations or rearrangements in the tandem long- (OPN1LW) and medium-wavelength (OPN1MW) cone opsin gene cluster. This cluster is located on the long arm of the X chromosome at cytogenetic band q28 (Xq28).

540919.long_answer: Biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the SMOC1 (Secreted Modular Calcium-binding protein 1) gene underlie syndromic microphthalmia type 7. Affected individuals present with very small eyeballs (microphthalmia/anophthalmia) together with characteristic cranio-facial deformities such as broad nasal bridge, cleft lip/palate and other facial dysmorphisms, establishing SMOC1 mutation as the causal genetic defect.

792852.long_answer: A distinctive collapsing form of focal segmental glomerulosclerosis—often termed HIV-associated nephropathy (HIVAN)—occurs in patients with AIDS. Numerous studies have demonstrated that direct infection of renal epithelial cells by HIV and expression of viral genes drive the characteristic pathological changes, firmly linking HIV to this pattern of glomerulosclerosis.

811755.long_answer: Rabson–Mendenhall syndrome results from biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the INSR (insulin receptor) gene, which is located on human chromosome 19p13.2. The same INSR mutations cause extreme hyperinsulinaemia that can trigger accelerated growth and early activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, leading to precocious puberty. Thus, the chromosome implicated in both Rabson–Mendenhall syndrome and mutation-related precocious puberty is chromosome 19.

190831.long_answer: The form of Acrofrontofacionasal (acromelic frontonasal) dysostosis that has been molecularly characterised is caused by heterozygous pathogenic variants in the ZSWIM6 gene. ZSWIM6 maps to cytogenetic location 5q12.3; hence the gene responsible for this disorder is situated on human chromosome 5.

381452.long_answer: A mutation in the FGFR2 gene is associated with Crouzon syndrome, a craniosynostosis disorder that often features mandibular prognathism due to premature fusion of cranial sutures altering mid-facial growth.

266850.long_answer: Joe McPhee released an album entitled “Old Eyes.” The term “old eyes” is the literal English translation of presbyopia, the common age-related condition in which the eye loses the ability to focus on nearby objects as the lens stiffens with age. Thus the album’s title shares the key term associated with this aging-eye condition.

522559.long_answer: Otospondylomegaepiphyseal dysplasia is caused by pathogenic variants in the COL11A2 gene. This gene is situated at cytogenetic band 6p21.3 on human chromosome 6, establishing chromosome 6 as the locus associated with the disorder.

108838.long_answer: GeneReviews is an authoritative, peer-reviewed online medical knowledge base hosted by the NCBI that provides comprehensive articles on genetic disorders. Each article details clinical presentation, molecular genetics, and available laboratory testing, guiding clinicians in selecting and interpreting genetic tests for conditions such as Trevor disease (dysplasia epiphysealis hemimelica).

532232.long_answer: Activating mutations in the FGFR3 gene cause achondroplasia, the most common genetic skeletal malformation syndrome (≈1 in 15–25 000 live births). Achondroplasia is far more frequent than Cousin syndrome, which is extremely rare and TBX15-related, making FGFR3 the gene linked to a skeletal malformation syndrome that is appreciably less rare than Cousin syndrome.

666423.long_answer: Gain-of-function mutations in the fibroblast growth factor receptor 2 (FGFR2) gene produce Beare–Stevenson cutis gyrata syndrome. This craniosynostosis syndrome presents with characteristic corrugated scalp folds termed cutis gyrata, along with acanthosis nigricans and mid-face hypoplasia. FGFR2 mutations (e.g., Tyr375Cys, Ser372Cys) enhance receptor signaling, driving abnormal skin and cranial bone development that underlies the cutis gyrata phenotype.

459366.long_answer: In multiple system atrophy, degeneration of brain-stem nuclei that control the laryngeal abductors can produce bilateral vocal cord (abductor) paralysis. This often presents early with inspiratory stridor during sleep or exertion and is one of the most frequent initial clinical manifestations of the disease.

424809.long_answer: Heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the MYCN gene cause Feingold syndrome. This autosomal-dominant disorder is characterized by microcephaly, digital anomalies, and gastrointestinal malformations, notably esophageal and/or duodenal atresia, making MYCN mutation the well-established genetic cause of a syndrome that includes esophageal atresia.

569511.long_answer: No context has been provided yet, so I cannot generate an evidence-based answer at this time. Please supply the relevant context.

979682.long_answer: The French neurologist Joseph Jules Dejerine was the first to introduce the term “olivopontocerebellar atrophy” (dégénérescence olivo-ponto-cérébelleuse) in 1900, when he described a familial neurodegenerative disorder characterized pathologically by atrophy of the inferior olives, pons and cerebellum—changes that later became recognized as one phenotypic expression of what we now call multiple system atrophy.

381575.long_answer: Coloboma can result from mutations in the CHD7 gene, which is located on chromosome 8q12.2. Pathogenic variants in CHD7 disrupt embryonic eye development and are a hallmark of CHARGE syndrome, where ocular coloboma is one of the core diagnostic features. Thus, chromosome 8 is the chromosome classically associated with a gene mutation leading to coloboma.

778785.long_answer: The disorder is iminoglycinuria, in which defective renal re-uptake of imino acids leads to massive urinary loss of glycine, proline and hydroxyproline. Loss-of-function mutations in the SLC36A2 gene, encoding the proton-coupled amino-acid transporter PAT2 that normally reabsorbs these amino acids in the proximal tubule, are the primary genetic cause; the impaired transporter cannot reclaim the filtered amino acids, so they are excreted in excess.

562393.long_answer: Limb-malformation syndromes in which both syndactyly and ulnar hypoplasia occur (e.g., HOXD13-related or ZRS/SHH–related limb anomalies) are typically seen in multiple successive generations, affect males and females equally, and show parent-to-child transmission without skipping generations. This pattern is characteristic of autosomal dominant inheritance.

801070.long_answer: The TNF (tumor necrosis factor-α) gene, located in the major histocompatibility complex on human chromosome 6 (6p21.3), plays a role in the inflammatory pathology of multiple sclerosis. It is the molecular target of monoclonal antibodies such as adalimumab that neutralize TNF-α to modulate immune responses.

667659.long_answer: Ornithine translocase deficiency, manifesting clinically as hyperornithinemia-hyperammonemia-homocitrullinuria (HHH) syndrome, results from pathogenic mutations in the SLC25A15 gene. SLC25A15 encodes the mitochondrial ornithine transporter 1 (ORNT1); loss-of-function variants impair the transport of ornithine into mitochondria, disrupting the urea cycle and leading to accumulation of ornithine, ammonia, and homocitrulline—hallmark biochemical features of the disorder.

101025.long_answer: Prolidase deficiency is caused by pathogenic variants in the PEPD (peptidase D) gene, which is mapped to cytogenetic band 19q13 on chromosome 19.

166026.long_answer: Variants in the PRDM5 gene cause Brittle Cornea Syndrome type 2, a connective-tissue disorder whose clinical triad includes progressive corneal dystrophy/fragility with severe photophobia and systemic skeletal abnormalities such as joint hypermobility, scoliosis, and bone fragility.

146230.long_answer: Fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva—historically termed myositis ossificans progressiva—presents with heterotopic bone formation in skeletal muscles, especially around the hip and shoulder girdles. This condition is caused by recurrent activating mutations in the ACVR1 (also known as ALK2) gene, which encodes the BMP type I receptor; the mutation dysregulates BMP signalling, driving ectopic ossification in affected muscles.

975468.long_answer: The constellation of orbital cysts, microphthalmia, porencephaly, agenesis of the corpus callosum, and facial skin tags defines oculocerebrocutaneous (Delleman–Oorthuys) syndrome. The marked male predominance and presumed lethality in non-mosaic females have led investigators to implicate an X-linked locus, making the X chromosome the prime candidate for harboring the causal gene(s).

587681.long_answer: Biallelic pathogenic variants in the MCOLN1 gene, which encodes the lysosomal cation channel mucolipin-1 (TRPML1), are responsible for mucolipidosis type IV—a lysosomal storage disorder whose cardinal clinical features include markedly delayed psychomotor development together with ocular abnormalities such as corneal clouding, retinal degeneration and visual impairment.

513661.long_answer: The designation FRAXD refers to a fragile-site locus on the X chromosome (fra(X)-D). Fragile sites are defined in cytogenetics as heritable chromosomal loci that are prone to the appearance of gaps, constrictions, or breaks when cells are cultured under particular conditions (e.g., folate deprivation, aphidicolin exposure). Because FRAXD is itself named as one of these fragile sites, it is, by definition, a heritable point on a chromosome that tends to form such gaps or breaks. Hence the statement is supported by established cytogenetic consensus.

390648.long_answer: Localised limb gigantism is a hallmark of Proteus syndrome. This overgrowth disorder is caused by a somatic, activating point mutation (most commonly c.49G>A, p.E17K) in the AKT1 gene. The mutant AKT1 drives excessive cell proliferation in affected tissue segments, resulting in progressive, asymmetric overgrowth and enlargement of portions of a limb.

880002.long_answer: Missense mutations in the FGFR2 gene, which encodes fibroblast growth factor receptor-2, cause Apert syndrome. This craniosynostosis disorder is clinically characterized by severe syndactyly of the fingers and toes, making FGFR2 mutations a well-established genetic cause of syndactyly.

955862.long_answer: A pathogenic mutation in the TCOF1 gene is responsible for Treacher-Collins (mandibulofacial dysostosis) syndrome, an autosomal-dominant disorder whose cardinal craniofacial features include severe micrognathia/micrognathism, hypoplastic zygomatic arches, and downward-slanting palpebral fissures. Loss-of-function variants in TCOF1 disrupt ribosome biogenesis in neural-crest cells, impairing mandibular and facial bone development and producing the characteristic small lower jaw.

453760.long_answer: Mulibrey nanism is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the TRIM37 gene. Cytogenetic mapping places TRIM37 at 17q22-q23 on human chromosome 17, making this chromosome the locus for the gene responsible for the disorder.

235777.long_answer: Mutations in the IFT80 gene, which is situated on human chromosome 3q13.33, are a well-established cause of Jeune asphyxiating thoracic dysplasia (also called asphyxiating thoracic dystrophy). Therefore, the chromosome that contains a gene associated with this disorder is chromosome 3.

252634.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the IKBKG gene, which encodes the NF-κB essential modulator (NEMO), cause incontinentia pigmenti. This disorder is inherited in an X-linked-dominant pattern, and hemizygous males lacking a normal IKBKG allele usually die in utero, so pregnancies with affected male fetuses frequently end as miscarriages or stillbirths.

107993.long_answer: The gene on chromosome 10q26 encodes the serine protease HTRA1; loss-of-function variants reduce HTRA1 activity and cause CARASIL (cerebral autosomal recessive arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy). One of the earliest and most characteristic clinical signs of CARASIL is premature alopecia—noticeable hair loss beginning in adolescence or early adulthood.

764164.long_answer: The papulosquamous disorder that can mimic Gianotti–Crosti syndrome is acrodermatitis enteropathica, an autosomal-recessive zinc-malabsorption disease. It is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the SLC39A4 gene, which encodes the ZIP4 zinc transporter. Identifying an SLC39A4 mutation distinguishes acrodermatitis enteropathica from Gianotti–Crosti syndrome.

811289.long_answer: Families reported with the triad of congenital thumb stiffness, brachydactyly, and intellectual disability show multiple affected siblings of both sexes born to clinically normal, often consanguineous parents and no male-to-male transmission. This segregation pattern is most consistent with an autosomal recessive mode of inheritance.

639159.long_answer: The disease 'Yaws' appears under the letter ‘Y’ in alphabetical lists of infectious diseases. It is caused by the bacterium Treponema pallidum subspecies pertenue, a spirochete closely related to the syphilis pathogen. This bacterium is transmitted through direct skin contact and produces chronic lesions of skin and bone, establishing it as the etiologic agent of the Y-listed disease.

875985.long_answer: Chronic cadmium poisoning (e.g., in the ‘Itai-itai’ disease of Japan) leads to renal tubular damage, impaired vitamin D activation, and loss of calcium and phosphate, producing bone demineralization and softening that clinically resembles osteomalacia.

464441.long_answer: The HBB gene (β-globin) is located on chromosome 11p15.5. Point mutations in HBB cause disorders such as β-thalassemia and sickle-cell disease. These hemoglobinopathies produce chronic, often severe anemia; to compensate for reduced oxygen delivery, the body increases heart rate, making sinus tachycardia a characteristic clinical sign. Thus, mutation of the HBB gene on chromosome 11 is directly linked to conditions in which tachycardia is a prominent symptom.

490188.long_answer: Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) uses fluorescently labeled DNA probes that bind to specific chromosome regions, allowing visualization of the chromosomal origin of small supernumerary marker chromosomes (sSMCs) and precise identification of the genetic material they contain.

329994.long_answer: The GYS2 gene, which encodes liver glycogen synthase and maps to chromosome 12p12.2, is mutated in glycogen storage disease type 0. This disorder impairs hepatic glycogen synthesis, leading to fasting hypoglycemia that, when severe, can precipitate seizures or coma.

443124.long_answer: An abscess is a localized collection of pus that develops during an acute inflammatory response to infection; while most abscesses are bacterial, they can also be produced by pathogenic fungi, making it an acute inflammatory process caused by a fungal infection. The symphonic-metal band Abscess adopted this medical term as its name, so the band’s title and the pathological entity are the same.

505393.long_answer: Shprintzen–Goldberg syndrome is caused by pathogenic variants in the SKI gene. Cytogenetic mapping places SKI on the short arm of human chromosome 1 (region 1p36), establishing chromosome 1 as the chromosomal location of the disease-causing gene.

242795.long_answer: No contextual information has been provided to derive the answer. Please supply the relevant passage or data so I can generate an accurate response strictly based on that context.

366570.long_answer: The gene MLYCD, which encodes malonyl-CoA decarboxylase—the enzyme that converts malonyl-CoA to acetyl-CoA and whose deficiency causes combined malonic and methylmalonic acidemias—is located on human chromosome 16 (band 16q24).

411994.long_answer: Achondrogenesis type 1A is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the TRIP11 gene, which encodes the Golgi microtubule-associated protein GMAP-210. GMAP-210 is essential for maintaining normal Golgi structure and trafficking; its absence disrupts Golgi organization, leading to the severe cartilage and bone dysplasia characteristic of achondrogenesis type 1A.

504687.long_answer: In Hirschsprung–polydactyly–deafness (HDPS) syndrome, multiple affected siblings are born to unaffected, often consanguineous parents and males and females are equally affected. This segregation pattern, together with absence of vertical transmission, establishes an autosomal-recessive mode of inheritance.

305834.long_answer: The subtype of Castleman disease linked to a virus is HHV-8–positive (Kaposi sarcoma–associated herpesvirus) multicentric Castleman disease. Human herpesvirus-8 not only drives this form of Castleman disease but also confers higher risk for HHV-8–related lymphomas such as primary effusion lymphoma.

570795.long_answer: Trismus–pseudocamptodactyly (Hecht) syndrome, an autosomal-dominant disorder marked by limited mouth opening (trismus) and distal musculoskeletal contractures, is caused by heterozygous missense mutations in the MYH8 gene, which encodes the perinatal skeletal-muscle myosin heavy chain. These mutations disrupt sarcomeric myosin function, leading to the characteristic musculoskeletal abnormalities.

132415.long_answer: In WAGR syndrome, aniridia results from deletion of the PAX6 gene, which is located at the 11p13 region of chromosome 11. Thus, chromosome 11 is the chromosome associated with the gene responsible for aniridia in this syndrome.

494338.long_answer: ADP is a physiologic platelet agonist that binds P2Y receptors and triggers inside-out signalling, converting the αIIbβ3 (GPIIb/IIIa) integrin into its active, fibrinogen-binding form. This integrin is absent or non-functional in Glanzmann’s thrombasthenia, so ADP fails to produce normal platelet aggregation in affected patients.

877935.long_answer: Epidemic typhus is a rickettsial disease caused by the obligate intracellular bacterium Rickettsia prowazekii. This pathogen is transmitted to humans primarily by the human body louse (Pediculus humanus corporis), and louse-borne spread can lead to large epidemics of typhus.

881562.long_answer: Klippel–Feil syndrome has been genetically linked to several genes involved in vertebral segmentation and bone development, most notably GDF6 (Growth Differentiation Factor 6) on chromosome 8q22.1 and MEOX1 on chromosome 17q21. No gene known to cause Klippel–Feil syndrome and contribute to vertebral bone development is located on chromosome 9. Therefore, the statement that such a gene resides on chromosome 9 is not supported by established genetic evidence.

538683.long_answer: Huntington’s disease is caused by an expanded CAG trinucleotide repeat in the HTT (huntingtin) gene. This gene is mapped to cytogenetic band 4p16.3 on the short arm of human chromosome 4, a location confirmed by decades of genetic linkage studies and all major genomic databases. It is not found on chromosome 6, so the statement is incorrect.

662723.long_answer: Human Granulocytic Anaplasmosis is caused by Anaplasma phagocytophilum, an obligate intracellular bacterium that specifically targets and infects neutrophils—one of the granulocytic white blood cells—where it resides within membrane-bound vacuoles and disrupts normal neutrophil functions.

901984.long_answer: Deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme arylsulfatase A blocks the degradation of cerebroside-3-sulfate, a sphingolipid. The resulting accumulation causes metachromatic leukodystrophy, a sphingolipidosis that presents with demyelination and neurological signs such as abnormal (diminished or exaggerated) reflexes, ataxia and peripheral neuropathy.

873577.long_answer: Candida species are not confined to causing superficial mucocutaneous infections; they can invade the bloodstream (candidemia) and disseminate hematogenously. Once in the circulation, the organisms can seed multiple organs—including the kidneys, liver, spleen, heart, eyes, and central nervous system—resulting in invasive or disseminated candidiasis. This systemic form of infection is well documented, particularly in immunocompromised individuals, patients with indwelling catheters, or those receiving broad-spectrum antibiotics. Therefore, Candida can indeed cause infections that affect multiple organs.

473564.long_answer: Syndromes characterized by congenital rib abnormalities—such as the short-rib polydactyly group—are classically inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern, meaning two pathogenic alleles (one from each parent) are required for disease expression.

973924.long_answer: Mutations in the HPGD gene (15-hydroxyprostaglandin dehydrogenase), located at 4q34-q35 on chromosome 4, are known to cause Pachydermoperiostosis and can also manifest with severe acne. Thus, the relevant gene resides on chromosome 4.

464587.long_answer: Sir Jonathan Hutchinson, an English surgeon and pathologist of the late 19th century, first described the diagnostic triad for congenital syphilis—Hutchinson’s teeth, interstitial keratitis, and eighth-nerve deafness—now universally known as Hutchinson’s triad.

510918.long_answer: Oogenesis is the meiotic process in female animals that converts diploid oogonia into a single haploid ovum. Errors in chromosome segregation (nondisjunction) during either meiotic division of oogenesis can lead to aneuploid gametes; fertilization with such an egg may produce monosomy X, the chromosomal basis of Turner syndrome.

595575.long_answer: Pachydermoperiostosis (primary hypertrophic osteoarthropathy) is most often caused by loss-of-function mutations in the HPGD gene, which encodes 15-hydroxyprostaglandin dehydrogenase. The HPGD gene is located on the long arm of human chromosome 4 (4q34–q35), making chromosome 4 the chromosomal location associated with Pachydermoperiostosis.

241786.long_answer: Mutations in the GPSM2 gene cause Chudley-McCullough syndrome, a rare autosomal-recessive disorder characterized by bilateral congenital sensorineural hearing loss together with distinct brain malformations such as hydrocephalus, cerebellar hypoplasia and corpus callosum abnormalities.

459251.long_answer: Mutations in the KCNQ2 gene, which encodes a voltage-gated potassium channel subunit, are the single most common genetic cause of neonatal-onset seizures that exhibit both tonic and clonic phases. KCNQ2 loss-of-function disrupts neuronal M-current, lowers seizure threshold, and underlies the majority of benign familial neonatal seizures and many cases of early-onset epileptic encephalopathy in newborns.

854675.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the COL3A1 gene, which encodes type III collagen, cause the vascular form of Ehlers–Danlos syndrome. This connective-tissue disorder is clinically distinguished by very thin, translucent skin that reveals underlying vasculature, reflecting defective synthesis of type III collagen.

456660.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the SMN1 gene cause spinal muscular atrophy (SMA). SMA is characterized by degeneration of lower motor neurons, leading to profound muscle weakness and marked neonatal or early-infantile hypotonia (‘floppy baby’ presentation).

230746.long_answer: Experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE) is an animal model of multiple-sclerosis-like central-nervous-system demyelination that can be induced by immunization with myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (MOG). The human demyelinating disorders characterized by serum anti-MOG antibodies (MOG-antibody–associated disease) share clinical and pathological features with EAE, linking anti-MOG antibodies directly to this experimentally modeled demyelinating disease.

841816.long_answer: Fragile X syndrome results from CGG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the FMR1 gene, which is situated at band Xq27.3 on the X chromosome. Because the gene is X-linked, males (who have a single X chromosome) are typically more severely affected than females.

328005.long_answer: Western equine encephalitis virus is primarily transmitted by mosquitoes of the genus Culex—especially Culex tarsalis—which act as vectors moving the virus between birds (the main amplifying hosts) and mammals, including horses and humans.

419172.long_answer: In Wieacker syndrome, a truncating mutation that substitutes the arginine residue at position 18 of the ZC4H2 protein (p.Arg18*) has been documented. This Arg18* mutation results in a loss-of-function that produces a lethal clinical phenotype, establishing arginine as the critical amino acid involved.

704991.long_answer: Marfan syndrome results from pathogenic variants in the FBN1 gene encoding fibrillin-1. The FBN1 gene is located on the long arm of chromosome 15 (15q21.1), making chromosome 15 the chromosome that carries the gene responsible for Marfan syndrome.

324379.long_answer: The TCN1 gene encodes haptocorrin (also called transcobalamin I or R-binder), a glycoprotein secreted in saliva and gastric juice that tightly binds dietary cobalamin in the acidic stomach environment. This binding shields vitamin B12 from acid degradation until pancreatic proteases release it in the duodenum for subsequent transfer to intrinsic factor.

526635.long_answer: In 22q11.2 deletion (DiGeorge/velocardiofacial) syndrome, loss of one copy of the TBX1 gene is regarded as the main contributor to many of the disorder’s features, including congenital heart defects, cleft palate, and characteristic craniofacial anomalies. TBX1 encodes a T-box transcription factor essential for pharyngeal arch and cardiac development, so haploinsufficiency of this single gene explains several of the clinical manifestations seen when the 22q11.2 region is deleted.

456705.long_answer: Nascimento syndrome (an X-linked form of intellectual disability characterized by developmental delay, speech impairment and dysmorphic features) is caused by loss-of-function mutations or deletions in the UBE2A gene, which encodes the ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme E2 A on the X chromosome.

743242.long_answer: The combination of thumb triphalangy, polysyndactyly and partial or complete tibial hypoplasia/aplasia defines the tibial hemimelia–triphalangeal thumb-polysyndactyly spectrum. This phenotype is consistently caused by pathogenic variants or duplications within the ZPA regulatory sequence (ZRS) that lies in intron 5 of the LMBR1 gene. Disruption of this enhancer alters Sonic hedgehog (SHH) expression during limb bud development, leading to the characteristic digital and tibial malformations. Hence, LMBR1 is the gene associated with this syndrome.

739590.long_answer: The genus Lentivirus (family Retroviridae) contains human immunodeficiency viruses HIV-1 and HIV-2, which infect humans, as well as numerous simian immunodeficiency viruses (SIVs) that infect chimpanzees, macaques, sooty mangabeys, and many other non-human primates. Thus, species within the Lentivirus genus naturally infect both humans and other primate hosts.

323861.long_answer: Phenylketonuria is caused by pathogenic variants in the PAH gene, which encodes the enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase. The PAH gene is located on the long arm of human chromosome 12 (12q23.2). Mutations impair Phe-to-Tyr conversion, leading to toxic phenylalanine accumulation that, if untreated, can shorten lifespan. Thus, chromosome 12 harbors the gene responsible for this disorder.

923133.long_answer: Grebe (acromesomelic) dysplasia results from loss-of-function mutations in the GDF5/CDMP1 gene, which is mapped to cytogenetic band 20q11.2 on chromosome 20. Therefore, chromosome 20 is the chromosome associated with the causative gene mutation.

386270.long_answer: GAA trinucleotide repeat expansion mutations in the FXN gene (encoding frataxin) cause Friedreich’s ataxia, a neurodegenerative disorder whose clinical picture classically includes progressive dysarthria along with gait ataxia, limb weakness and loss of proprioception.

430479.long_answer: I’m sorry, but I don’t have any context to answer this question. Please provide the relevant passage or data, and I will use only that to generate the answer.

225246.long_answer: Cantú syndrome is most commonly caused by gain-of-function mutations in the ABCC9 gene, which encodes the SUR2 subunit of ATP-sensitive potassium channels. The ABCC9 gene is situated on the short arm of chromosome 12 (12p12.1). Pathogenic variants in this locus lead to the characteristic features of Cantú syndrome, thus placing the responsible gene on chromosome 12.

997146.long_answer: DFNB1, the most common form of autosomal-recessive nonsyndromic hearing loss caused by mutations in the GJB2 gene (connexin 26), has been mapped to the long arm of human chromosome 13 (13q11-q12). Therefore, the gene responsible for connexin 26-related deafness resides on chromosome 13.

454126.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the progranulin gene (GRN) are the clearest genetic cause of the non-fluent/agrammatic variant of primary progressive aphasia, a form that impairs both speech production (effortful, agrammatic output) and syntactic comprehension. GRN haploinsufficiency leads to TDP-43-positive frontotemporal lobar degeneration, and numerous family studies have consistently demonstrated this mutation–phenotype association.

561522.long_answer: Type 2A Megalencephalic leukoencephalopathy with subcortical cysts (MLC2A) results from recessive mutations in the HEPACAM (GlialCAM) gene. HEPACAM is located on the long arm of human chromosome 11 at 11q24, so the gene associated with MLC type 2A resides on chromosome 11.

838802.long_answer: The first gene shown to cause Seckel syndrome is ATR, which is mapped to cytogenetic band 3q23 on human chromosome 3.

960630.long_answer: A research group at the University of Hawaii (John A. Burns School of Medicine) first identified mutations in the ABCC6 gene on chromosome 16 as the molecular cause of Pseudoxanthoma elasticum, thereby pinpointing the genetic basis for this connective-tissue disorder.

540085.long_answer: Rothmund-Thomson syndrome, an autosomal-recessive disorder characterized early by facial and acral poikiloderma, is caused by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the RECQL4 DNA helicase gene.

291912.long_answer: Théophile Alajouanine (with Charles Foix) first described the condition now called Foix–Alajouanine syndrome, a subacute necrotic myelopathy caused by a dural arteriovenous malformation of the spinal cord that produces venous congestion and progressive neurological deficits.

368881.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the XYLT2 gene, which encodes xylosyl-transferase-II required for proteoglycan biosynthesis, cause the autosomal-recessive disorder known as spondylo-ocular syndrome. This syndrome is typified by flattened, deformed vertebrae (platyspondyly), global developmental delay, and characteristic ocular defects that include congenital cataract or lens coloboma. Hence, mutation of XYLT2 is the established genetic basis of the described clinical picture.

820878.long_answer: Chediak-Higashi syndrome is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the LYST (also known as CHS1) gene. The disease presents with partial oculocutaneous albinism, which reduces iris and retinal pigment and results in marked photophobia, in addition to recurrent infections and giant lysosomal granules in leukocytes.

243843.long_answer: Mutations in the EBP gene (encoding emopamil-binding protein, a sterol isomerase) cause Conradi-Hünermann-Happle syndrome, also known as X-linked dominant chondrodysplasia punctata type 2. This disorder is characterized by epiphyseal stippling (chondrodysplasia punctata) and can present at birth as a collodion baby because of generalized ichthyosiform erythroderma, linking the EBP gene to both clinical features.

989484.long_answer: Mutations in the RUNX2 gene cause cleidocranial dysplasia, a skeletal (bone) disorder characterized by defective clavicle and craniofacial development. The craniofacial abnormalities frequently produce dental crowding, delayed tooth eruption, and altered jaw growth, all of which can result in malocclusion.

138394.long_answer: Heterozygous gain‐of‐function mutations in the STAT3 gene cause a condition known as STAT3 gain-of-function disease. This primary immunoregulatory disorder is characterized by early-onset, multi-organ autoimmunity and/or combined immunodeficiency, and it carries a high risk of severe, life-threatening infections and immune-mediated organ damage that can lead to premature death.

271994.long_answer: The two causative genes for Epidermodysplasia verruciformis, EVER1 (TMC6) and EVER2 (TMC8), are physically clustered in the 17q25 region of chromosome 17. Loss-of-function mutations in either of these adjacent genes impair keratinocyte immunity to specific β-human papillomaviruses, producing the characteristic lesions of the disease. Hence, chromosome 17 harbors the genes associated with Epidermodysplasia verruciformis.

473719.long_answer: The shallow eye sockets and resultant exophthalmos seen in craniosynostosis disorders such as Crouzon syndrome are produced by pathogenic mutations in the FGFR2 (fibroblast growth factor receptor-2) gene; these gain-of-function mutations disturb skull suture development, leading to premature fusion of cranial sutures and the characteristic shallow orbits.

821893.long_answer: Mutations in the SEPN1 gene, which encodes the endoplasmic-reticulum selenoprotein N, are responsible for SEPN1-related myopathy (also called rigid spine muscular dystrophy type 1). This congenital neuromuscular disorder presents with gradually worsening muscle stiffness and pronounced axial rigidity, especially of the spine, due to impaired muscle calcium homeostasis and resistance to oxidative stress caused by loss of functional selenoprotein N.

291834.long_answer: Mutations in the OTC gene impair the enzyme ornithine transcarbamylase, a key catalyst in the urea cycle. Loss of this enzymatic activity blocks conversion of carbamoyl-phosphate and ornithine to citrulline, causing ammonia to accumulate in blood and resulting in the metabolic disorder known as ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency.

703070.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the POMGNT1 gene (protein-O-mannose β-1,2-N-acetylglucosaminyltransferase 1) cause the Muscle-Eye-Brain form of congenital muscular dystrophy. Because defective glycosylation of α-dystroglycan affects both skeletal muscle and the central nervous system, affected individuals show congenital hypotonia and muscle weakness together with cortical malformations that frequently manifest as epileptic seizures featuring myoclonus.

953087.long_answer: The gene UBR1, whose mutations cause Johanson–Blizzard syndrome and can also manifest with aplasia cutis congenita of the scalp, is located on human chromosome 15 (cytogenetic band 15q15.2). Thus, chromosome 15 harbors the gene linked to both conditions.

886512.long_answer: The primary gene implicated in Megalencephalic leukoencephalopathy with subcortical cysts is MLC1, which has been mapped to the long arm of human chromosome 22 (22q13.3). Pathogenic variants in MLC1 on chromosome 22 are the classical cause of this leukodystrophy.

894693.long_answer: HSAN IE is linked to mutations in the DNMT1 gene, which encodes DNA (cytosine-5)-methyltransferase 1. DNMT1’s canonical role is the maintenance of DNA methylation patterns immediately after DNA replication, a process that takes place during the S phase of the cell cycle. Therefore, the enzyme’s key activity is specifically associated with the S phase.

516286.long_answer: Roberts syndrome is produced by pathogenic mutations in the ESCO2 gene. Cytogenetic and molecular mapping place ESCO2 on the short arm of human chromosome 8 (region 8p21.1). Therefore, the gene responsible for Roberts syndrome—and the associated feature of exophthalmos—is located on chromosome 8.

335838.long_answer: Hereditary hair disorders that are apparent at birth or in early infancy are typically assessed by pediatric dermatologists. This subspecialty of dermatology focuses on skin, hair, and nail diseases in children and uses clinical examination, dermoscopy, scalp biopsy, and genetic testing to diagnose congenital hair conditions.

737991.long_answer: A disproportionately large number of genes that, when mutated, cause X-linked intellectual disability are located on the X chromosome. Well-characterized examples include FMR1 (Fragile X syndrome), MECP2 (Rett syndrome), and ARX, illustrating that this chromosome harbors the greatest concentration of genes whose defects lead to inherited cognitive impairment.

254428.long_answer: DiGeorge syndrome—also called 22q11.2 deletion syndrome or velocardiofacial syndrome—is produced by a microdeletion on chromosome 22q11.2. Loss of genes in this region disrupts normal craniofacial development, leading to characteristic features that include hypertelorism, along with conotruncal heart defects, thymic hypoplasia, and hypocalcaemia.

484583.long_answer: The missense mutation c.338C>T (p.Ser113Leu) in the CPT2 gene on chromosome 1p32 is the most common genetic defect causing carnitine palmitoyltransferase II deficiency, a fatty-acid‐oxidation disorder characterized clinically by recurrent episodes of myalgia, muscle weakness, and rhabdomyolysis following prolonged exercise or fasting.

574909.long_answer: The syndrome that combines congenital scalp defects (classically aplasia cutis congenita) with type A post-axial polydactyly is most commonly Adams-Oliver syndrome. The great majority of Adams-Oliver cases are transmitted in an autosomal dominant manner through heterozygous pathogenic variants in genes such as ARHGAP31, DLL4, NOTCH1 or RBPJ. Thus, the characteristic inheritance pattern for this disorder is autosomal dominant.

667646.long_answer: DFNB1 deafness is caused by pathogenic variants in the GJB2 (connexin-26) gene, which is located on the long arm of human chromosome 13 (region 13q11-q12).

817588.long_answer: Hermaphroditic organisms possess both male and female reproductive organs and can generate both sperm and eggs, enabling them to produce both types of gametes within the same individual.

156962.long_answer: Guanidinoacetate methyltransferase (GAMT) deficiency is caused by mutations in the GAMT gene located at 19p13.3. Chromosome 19 is one of the numbered, non-sex (autosomal) chromosomes, so the disorder is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. Therefore, the gene responsible for GAMT deficiency resides on an autosomal chromosome rather than on a sex chromosome.

780228.long_answer: The syndrome produced by the 22q11.2 microdeletion (DiGeorge/velocardio-facial syndrome) deletes one copy of several genes. Among them, loss of a single functional copy of the transcription-factor gene TBX1 (haploinsufficiency) is strongly implicated in many of the characteristic features—especially the cardiac outflow-tract defects, craniofacial anomalies, and thymus-parathyroid hypoplasia—seen in patients with this chromosome-22 deletion syndrome.
